title: Job-Finding Anomalies of the Current Expansion - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed research finds U.S. job-finding rates have fallen for three years despite low unemployment, with the unemployed-to-employed rate down from 30% to 25% and the nonparticipant rate from 4.9% to 4.2% since January 2023. The demographic signature is inverted versus a normal expansion and versus 2007-09: the unemployment pipeline weakened most for prime-age and college-educated workers (-30% for college grads), while the nonparticipation pipeline weakened most for the young and less-educated, pointing to structural forces including possible early AI-related displacement in professional occupations.

themes.theme: Job finding falling inside an expansion

insights.claim: U.S. job-finding rates have fallen for three straight years despite a low unemployment rate, an unusual pattern for a mature economic expansion rather than a recession.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: Headline unemployment understates labor-market cooling; watch flows, not just the U-3 print, for turn signals.
insights.quote: Job-finding rates have declined since early 2023, an unusual development for a stable economy.

insights.claim: Between the January 2023 peak and January 2026, the monthly job-finding rate for unemployed U.S. workers fell from 30% to 25% and the rate for nonparticipants fell from 4.9% to 4.2%.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: A ~17% drop in the unemployed-to-employed rate means longer unemployment durations ahead even before the jobless rate rises.
insights.quote: The rate for nonparticipants fell from 4.9% to 4.2%, while the rate for unemployed workers fell from 30% to 25%.
insights.locator: Coming out of the pandemic recession

insights.claim: Falling transition rates from both unemployment and nonparticipation mean the labor market is simultaneously failing to absorb active job seekers and failing to pull people off the sidelines.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Two independent flow channels weakening at once argues the softening is real and broad in mechanism, not a statistical artifact.
insights.quote: The recent decline suggests that the labor market is neither efficiently absorbing the unemployed nor drawing in nonparticipants.

themes.theme: Two nonemployment pools as a diagnostic framework

insights.claim: Job-finding rates split into two distinct diagnostics: the unemployment-to-employment rate measures whether demand is strong enough to absorb active searchers, while the nonparticipation-to-employment rate measures whether opportunity is abundant enough to pull marginal workers in from the sidelines.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Gives a two-dimensional read on labor demand that the unemployment rate alone cannot provide.
insights.quote: A high unemployment-to-employment transition rate signals that demand is strong to absorb active job seekers quickly.
insights.locator: People without a job fall into two categories

insights.claim: Nonparticipants have a job-finding rate of only 4–5% versus 25–30% for the unemployed, yet they account for two-thirds of all monthly transitions from nonemployment into employment because their pool is so much larger.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Most hiring comes from outside the measured unemployed pool, so labor-supply analysis keyed only to the unemployment rate misses the majority of the flow.
insights.quote: nonparticipants make up two-thirds of all people who transition from nonemployment to employment each month on average

insights.claim: A shift-share decomposition of the January 2023 to January 2026 change shows the drop in job finding from unemployment is driven almost entirely by falling within-group rates, not by a compositional shift toward groups that normally find work slowly.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Rules out the benign 'mix effect' explanation; something is genuinely reducing hiring probability per worker.
insights.quote: We find that the decline in job-finding rates from unemployment reflects mostly rate decline by age and education groups and not compositional changes towards groups with typically lower rates.
insights.locator: Which groups are less successful at finding work?

insights.claim: The decline in job finding from nonparticipation is partly compositional, reflecting a shift toward an older nonparticipant population, unlike the unemployment channel.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Some of the sidelines weakness is demographic aging rather than deteriorating demand, so the two channels should not be read as one signal.
insights.quote: The decline in job-finding rates from nonparticipation reflects rate declines by age and education groups as well as some contribution from a compositional change towards an older population.
insights.locator: Which groups are less successful at finding work?

themes.theme: The skilled-worker pipeline is the one that broke

insights.claim: The decline in job finding out of unemployment is concentrated among college-educated workers, whose job-finding rate fell 30%, versus an 18% decline for some-college workers and an outright increase for those with less than a high school education.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Inverted education gradient: the credential premium in hiring speed is compressing, with implications for white-collar wage growth and consumption at the top of the income distribution.
insights.quote: College-educated individuals saw a decline of 30%, those with some college degree declined 18%, while workers with less than high school saw their job-finding rate increase.
insights.locator: By contrast, the decline in job finding from unemployment

insights.claim: The unemployment job-finding decline is largest for prime working ages 35–54, the cohort that normally finds work fastest even in weak labor markets.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Prime-age displacement is the group with the highest debt service and consumption commitments, raising the credit-sensitivity of any further deterioration.
insights.quote: The current decline from unemployment is concentrated among groups that typically have the highest job-finding rates: prime-age and college-educated workers.
insights.locator: The current decline from unemployment is concentrated

insights.claim: The authors argue the weakening of the unemployment-to-employment pipeline for skilled workers looks structural rather than cyclical, pointing to technology-related downsizing, managerial restructuring, government contractor reductions, or early AI-related displacement in professional occupations.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: A Fed research shop explicitly naming AI displacement as a candidate mechanism is an early institutional marker for the white-collar-automation trade.
insights.quote: the early effects of AI-related displacement in professional occupations
insights.locator: The changes in job-finding rates by age and education

insights.claim: Because the workers losing hiring speed are the ones who normally find jobs quickly regardless of the cycle, the pattern cannot be explained by a standard cyclical slowdown.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Argues against reading soft hiring data as a straightforward recession signal that rate cuts would fix.
insights.quote: The drop in their job-finding rates is particularly surprising and suggests something other than a standard cyclical slowdown.

themes.theme: The sidelines are no longer being pulled in

insights.claim: Job finding from nonparticipation fell 20% for ages 16–24 and 16% for ages 25–34 while barely moving for ages 35–64, and fell 23% for high school graduates and 19% for those with less than high school while not declining at all for bachelor's-degree holders.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Youth and low-credential entry into employment is closing first — a leading indicator for consumer stress at the low end.
insights.quote: Individuals ages 16–24 saw a 20% decline and those ages 25–34 fell 16%, while the job-finding rates of those ages 35–64 changed little
insights.locator: The decline in job finding from nonparticipation

insights.claim: The 'pulling-in' effect — where a lengthening recovery draws in younger, less-educated and less-experienced workers who could not find jobs in a weaker economy — is the hallmark of a mature expansion, and it is now running in reverse.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: The canonical high-pressure-economy benefit to marginal workers has stopped operating, which undercuts the case that keeping the expansion going will fix distributional labor outcomes.
insights.quote: Instead of being pulled in, the pipeline into employment is shrinking such that the recovery is no longer reaching workers at the margins.

insights.claim: Weaker job finding among traditionally marginal workers may simply be normalization from extraordinarily strong post-pandemic labor demand rather than fresh deterioration.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: A benign alternative reading of the low-end weakness; the two channels may require different policy responses.
insights.quote: Job finding among nonparticipants weakened for traditionally marginal workers, which may reflect a normalization following extraordinarily strong post-pandemic labor demand.
insights.locator: The changes in job-finding rates by age and education

themes.theme: Contrast with the Great Recession template

insights.claim: The current three-year job-finding decline is roughly half the size of the December 2006 to December 2009 episode, when the unemployment-to-employment rate fell about 13 percentage points (a 45% decrease) and the nonparticipation-to-employment rate fell 1.3 percentage points (a 24% decrease).
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Scales the current deterioration: meaningful but far from crisis magnitude, so recession-analog positioning on flows alone is premature.
insights.quote: The unemployment-to-employment job-finding rate dropped about 13 percentage points, a 45% decrease—more than double the current decline.
insights.locator: Putting the job-finding decline into historical perspective

insights.claim: The 2006–09 job-finding collapse hit all education levels roughly alike, whereas the current decline is education-polarized — concentrated among the less-educated from nonparticipation and among the more-educated from unemployment.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: The demographic signature is the tell: this is not a demand shock with a familiar shape, so recession playbooks may misprice which sectors and consumer cohorts get hit.
insights.quote: The 2006–09 declines in job-finding rates from nonparticipation and especially from unemployment were experienced across all education levels
insights.locator: We find sharp differences in job-finding rate changes

insights.claim: During the 2007–09 comparison period the U.S. unemployment rate rose from 4.4% to 9.9%, making the steep job-finding collapse of that era expected, in contrast to today's decline occurring with unemployment still relatively low.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Benchmarks how anomalous the current combination of low unemployment and falling job finding really is.
insights.quote: the unemployment rate rose from 4.4% to 9.9%
insights.locator: These large declines in both rates were expected

insights.claim: The San Francisco Fed authors flag immigration-driven changes, sector-specific slowdowns in technology and government contracting, policy uncertainty, and early broad labor-market deterioration as the leading candidate explanations still to be tested.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: A checklist of the variables to monitor for confirmation of the structural thesis; tech and federal-contractor hiring data are the cleanest tests.
insights.quote: including immigration-driven changes, sector-specific slowdowns in technology and government contracting, policy uncertainty, or early signals of broader labor market deterioration

insights.claim: The combined evidence implies the labor market is undergoing both a cooling and a restructuring, not merely a slowdown along a single dimension.
insights.speaker: Ingrid Chen
insights.so_what: Restructuring implies displaced skilled workers do not simply get rehired when demand recovers, extending the tail of any labor weakness.
insights.quote: imply both a cooling and a restructuring within the labor market
insights.locator: Job-finding rates have declined over the past three years
